extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)/(c)/(d) issues — especially on-sale and public-use bars, experimental-use exceptions, abandonment, and foreign-priority (102(d)) rejections. Intended to direct examiners and practitioners in assessing objective facts, intent, control, and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use doctrine — primary purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is whether the primary purpose of the inventor at the time of the sale was to conduct experimentation; experimentation must be the primary purpose and any commercial exploitation must be incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote and case law: Allen Eng’g Corp. v. Bartell Indus.; EZ Dock v. Schafer Sys. Experimental use means a bona fide effort to perfect the invention or to ascertain whether it will answer its intended purpose. If any commercial exploitation occurs it must be merely incidental. Market testing to gauge consumer demand is not experimental (In re Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial exploitation / on-sale/public-use policy
rubrics_metrics.description: One policy of the on-sale and public-use bars is prevention of inventors commercially exploiting inventions more than 1 year prior to filing; if precritical date activity is a sale or offer to sell that attempts market penetration, a patent is barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even bona fide experimental activity will not permit commercial exploitation beyond the 1-year grace period. Case: In re Theis. Examiner should treat offers/sales aimed at market penetration as statutory bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial activity must advance development toward completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial activity asserted as experimental must legitimately advance development of the invention toward completion; higher degrees of commercial exploitation increase an applicant's burden to establish clear and convincing evidence of experimental purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where examiner finds prima facie sale/offer to sell, applicant rarely meets burden unless necessity for experimentation is clearly shown. Sale can be permitted only if primary purpose is experimental; careful objective scrutiny required. Cases: In re Theis; Robbins Co.; Ushakoff; Cloud v. Standard Packaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors indicative of commercial exploitation (indicia of subjective intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia of an inventor’s subjective intent to commercially exploit include contemporaneous commercial documents, price lists/quotations, display of samples, demonstrations/models (especially at trade shows), charging admission for use, and advertising/publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of activities: (A) orders, invoices, receipts, delivery schedules; (B) price lists and distribution of price quotations; (C) display of samples to prospective customers; (D) demonstrations of models/prototypes (incl. trade conventions), even without orders; (E) use where admission fee charged; (F) advertising, publicity releases, brochures, periodicals. Case citations provided for each indicium. See MPEP §2133.03(e)(4) for experimental-purpose factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent — objective evidence required; secret subjective intent insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor's secretly held subjective belief that sales are experimental is unavailing without objective evidence; where sales occur in ordinary commercial environments and goods are placed outside inventor's control, the customer must be made aware of the experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must supply objective evidence of experimental intent; mere secret belief does not overcome prima facie bar. Cases: LaBounty Mfg.; Harrington Mfg.; Paragon Podiatry (sale of completed devices to trade without disclosure insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of the invention — experimentation ends at reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use ends when the invention is actually reduced to practice; proof that an inventor considered the invention 'complete' is strong evidence that experimental use ceased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice indicates experimental use ended; awaiting third-party approvals (e.g., Underwriters’ Laboratories) usually will not overcome evidence that invention was complete. Lack of subsequent modifications is evidence (though not conclusive) that activity was not experimental. Cases: RCA Corp.; Interroyal; Skil Corp.; In re Theis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition/disposal of prototypes
rubrics_metrics.description: If an inventor disposes of a prototype before the critical date, inquiry focuses on inventor intent and reasonableness of disposal; unrestricted disposal of a prototype considered 'complete' and with experimentation ceased constitutes a statutory bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidental income from reasonable disposal is not necessarily fatal, but if prototype was 'complete' and experimentation ended, unrestricted disposal is a 102(b) bar. Cases: In re Dybel; In re Blaisdell; Watson v. Allen (contra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors indicative of experimental purpose (13-factor list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider multiple factors to determine whether an on-sale/public-use was for experimentation rather than commercial exploitation: (1) necessity for public testing, (2) amount of control retained by inventor, (3) nature of the invention, (4) length of test period, (5) whether payment was made, (6) secrecy obligation, (7) whether records were kept, (8) who conducted experiment, (9) degree of commercial exploitation during testing, (10) whether invention reasonably requires evaluation under actual conditions, (11) whether testing was systematically performed, (12) whether inventor continually monitored the invention during testing, (13) nature of contacts with potential customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customer’s awareness of purported testing is a critical attribute. No single factor or particular combination is necessarily determinative; examiner must assess scope and length of activity as reasonable for claimed experimental purpose. Cases: Allen Eng’g; EZ Dock; Electromotive Div. of GM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation — degree of supervision and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor must maintain sufficient control and supervision over the invention during third-party testing; control and customer awareness ordinarily must be proven for experimentation to be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor relinquishes supervision and control without restraints, unrestricted subsequent use constitutes a 102(b) bar. Cases: Electromotive Div. v. GM; In re Blaisdell. Examiner should evaluate extent of inventor monitoring and contractual restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted experimental activity — developmental testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing in the normal context of technological development and experimentation to determine utility is generally permitted experimental activity under 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: continued testing of a chemical composition with no known utility would likely be permissible absent a sale or other evidence of commercial exploitation. Case: General Motors v. Bendix Aviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not permitted — market testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimentation to determine product acceptance (market testing) is commercial exploitation and not within the experimental-use exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market testing is typical of a trader, not an inventor. Testing to appease a customer or minor tune-ups requiring only technician skills are not within exception. Cases: Smith & Davis; In re Theis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental activity in design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Public display of an ornamental design to generate consumer interest is not experimental use; however, experimentation directed to functional features of a product that also has ornamental design may negate public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display for aesthetics is public use (In re Mann). Functional testing in context of a product that has ornamentation may be experimental if focused on function (Tone Brothers v. Sysco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception is personal to the applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of experimental activity by a party other than the applicant will not overcome a prima facie 102(b) bar unless the activity was under the supervision and control of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental-use showing by independent third parties is insufficient absent applicant supervision/control. Cases: Magnetics v. Arnold Eng’g; Bourne v. Jones; Watson v. Allen (contrast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) — abandonment requires intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual abandonment requires that the inventor intend to abandon the invention; intent can be implied from conduct, and every reasonable doubt should be resolved in favor of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay alone is insufficient to infer requisite intent to abandon. Case: In re Gibbs; Ex parte Dunne. Examples and contrary fact patterns are discussed (Moore; Davis Harvester).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in reapplying after abandonment of previous application
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay in reapplying for a patent after abandonment of a previous application does not necessarily constitute abandonment under 102(c) where there is no evidence of an expressed intent to abandon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no conduct or expression indicates abandonment, mere lapse in time after an abandoned application is insufficient to find abandonment. Case: Petersen v. Fee Int’l.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure in prior issued patent without claiming — rebuttable inference of abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of subject matter in a prior issued patent but not claimed does not automatically imply abandonment of that subject matter; any inference of abandonment is rebuttable by filing an application before a statutory bar arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection under 102(c) based solely on issuance of a patent that discloses but does not claim the subject matter is improper absent copendency between the applications. Case: In re Gibbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lapse of time does not bar patent except in priority contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere lapse of time will not bar a patent except when there is a priority contest under 102(g) and applicant abandons, suppresses, or conceals the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment, suppression, and concealment are treated under 102(g); in priority disputes lapse of time may be relevant. Case: Panduit Corp. v. Dennison Mfg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — four statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Four conditions establish a 102(d) bar: (A) the foreign application was filed more than 12 months before the effective U.S. filing date; (B) the foreign application was filed by the same applicant or legal representative/assigns; (C) the foreign patent or inventor's certificate was actually granted before the U.S. filing date; (D) the same invention is involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all four are present, the foreign patent may be used to bar a U.S. patent. Examiner should verify effective U.S. filing date (see MPEP §706.02) and check grant date and applicant identity. See MPEP §2135.01 for further clarification and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(d) — anniversary date on weekend/holiday extends to next business day
rubrics_metrics.description: If the 1-year anniversary of the foreign filing date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, the year is extended to the next business day for purposes of avoiding a 102(d) bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. application filed on the 1-year anniversary (with extension rules) is timely. Case/example: Ex parte Olah. Note interplay with 37 CFR 1.6(a)(2) and 1.10 deposit rules and applicant's right to defer filing to next business day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation-in-part (CIP) breaks chain of priority for foreign and U.S. parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a CIP that includes new subject matter not entitled to the parent filing date breaks the chain of priority; the CIP's effective filing date governs and applicant may lose benefit of foreign or U.S. parent filing dates for claims not supported by the parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a foreign application issues into a patent before the CIP filing date, the foreign patent may be used in a 102(d)/103 rejection against CIP claims that are not entitled to parent filing dates. Case: In re Van Langenhoven; Ex parte Appeal No. 242-47.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(d) — foreign application must be filed by same applicant/representative/assigns (multiple inventors nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The foreign application must be filed by the same applicant (or their legal representative/assigns); where a U.S. application names multiple inventors, it is permissible that separate foreign applications filed to different inventors confer priority to corresponding inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should verify identity/ownership chain; separate foreign filings to different inventors or subsets may supply priority for corresponding claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: To be 'patented' under 102(d) an exclusionary right must be awarded
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Patented' means a formal bestowal of patent rights from the sovereign to the applicant — an exclusionary right must be awarded for the reference to be used under 102(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: German Gebrauchsmuster (petty patent) was treated as a patent for 102(d) purposes despite differences in term/examination. Case: In re Monks; American Infra-Red Radiant Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published foreign application is not generally a 'patent' for 102(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: A published foreign application (e.g., kokai, kohyo, Offenlegungsschriften) is generally not a 'patent' under pre-AIA 102(d) and therefore not usable as a 102(d) reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board cases: Ex parte Fujishiro; Ex parte Links. Publication alone typically does not equal grant; provisional rights are not sufficient unless other conditions met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed foreign application published for opposition can sometimes function as a 'patent' for 102(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examined foreign application that has been allowed and published for opposition may be treated as a 'patent' for 102(d) purposes as of the publication-for-opposition date if substantial provisional enforcement rights arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ex parte Beik (German Auslegeschrift). If the publication confers provisional enforcement rights substantially similar to a granted patent, it can trigger 102(d) as of that publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant date = date patent becomes enforceable; secrecy after grant does not avoid 102(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical date for a foreign patent as a 102(d) reference is the date the patent becomes enforceable (issued/sealed/granted); periods of secrecy after grant do not prevent application of 102(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Monks; In re Kathawala; Gramme Elec. Co. Secrecy options in some countries do not negate the grant date being the relevant reference date for 102(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(d) — 'same invention' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Same invention' means the subject matter claimed in the U.S. application could have been presented in the foreign patent; claims need not be identical and may be of different statutory classes if the foreign specification supports the U.S. claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the foreign patent fully discloses the invention and provides options supporting U.S. claims, 102(d) applies even if the foreign claims differ. Case: In re Kathawala (Spanish patent disclosing compounds/methods supported composition claims in U.S.). Examiner should assess whether foreign specification supports claimed U.S. subject matter.
